The Light-mantled albatross initiates breeding at a relatively advanced age, with first reproduction typically occurring at five years after hatching [tR = five years after hatching] under the thermal regime typical of active metabolism in this species, 39.4 °C [T = 39.4 °C]. This delayed onset of breeding is consistent with the slow pace of life characteristic of large procellariiform seabirds. Egg incubation, carried out by both parents in alternating shifts, proceeds at a temperature of 36 °C [T = 36 °C] and requires an average period of 66.6 days [ab = 66.6 days] before hatching occurs; this relatively protracted incubation interval reflects the energetic constraints imposed by foraging trips that may span hundreds of kilometers. The single egg produced per breeding attempt weighs approximately 259.2 grams, a substantial investment that represents a significant proportion of the female's body reserves. Following hatching, the chick is brooded closely for the first several weeks before being left alone for increasing durations as the parents forage.

At the core body temperature characteristic of active adults, measured at 39.4 °C [T = 39.4 °C], the fledgling chick departs the nest at approximately 103 days after hatching [tx = approximately 103 days after hatching], having achieved the wing feather development and body mass necessary for sustained flight. This milestone marks the end of the extended parental provisioning period that characterizes this species. The fledging mass reached prior to departure, approximately 3000 grams [Wwi = approximately 3000 grams], reflects a considerable growth trajectory from the modest hatchling size. Neonates emerge from the egg at a wet weight at birth of approximately 230 grams [Wwb = approximately 230 grams], a size that necessitates intensive biparental provisioning throughout the nestling period. This initial mass is modest relative to the ultimate asymptotic mass achieved prior to fledging, which averages about 2848 grams in adults. Growth rates during the early nestling phase are heavily influenced by the frequency of meal delivery from foraging adults, which in turn depends on oceanic productivity and prevailing wind conditions around the subantarctic breeding colonies. The discrepancy between the moderate egg weight and the substantial fledging mass underscores the critical role of marine resources during the chick-rearing period. Field studies have documented considerable interannual variation in chick growth trajectories, linked to fluctuations in sea surface temperature and prey availability. Reproductive output is consequently constrained by these environmental variables, with successful breeding occurring in fewer than half of all breeding attempts in some years.

During the period of sustained adult body temperature of 39.4 °C [T = 39.4 °C], maximum recorded longevity in this species reaches approximately 35 years [am = approximately 35 years], a lifespan that is among the longest documented for any procellariiform bird of comparable body size. Such extended lifespans are typical of pelagic seabirds that face low annual adult mortality once they reach breeding age. The reproductive strategy of the Light-mantled albatross is characterized by a low annual reproductive rate; females produce a single egg per clutch [N_R_i = single egg per clutch] and typically attempt to breed only once per year [F_R_i = attempt to breed only once per year], a schedule that reflects the high energetic cost of egg production and chick rearing. This combination of deferred maturity, single-egg clutches, and infrequent breeding attempts yields an exceptionally low maximum reproductive rate when considered across the entire lifespan, consistent with the species' placement at the slow end of the life-history continuum among seabirds. The trade-off between current reproductive investment and future survival probability is particularly acute in this species.

The mean adult body mass of 2848 grams observed in breeding individuals provides context for understanding the species' energetic demands and foraging ecology. This substantial size, combined with the protracted developmental periods described, positions the Light-mantled albatross as a classic example of a long-lived, slow-breeding pelagic species. Comparative analyses within the genus Phoebetria reveal that both the duration of parental care and the age at first breeding are similar between the two species, although subtle differences in wing loading and foraging strategy exist. The extended incubation period of 66.6 days [ab = 66.6 days] at 36 °C [T = 36 °C] is a critical determinant of overall breeding success, as longer incubation increases the risk of egg predation and storm damage at exposed nest sites on subantarctic islands. Future work examining the physiological mechanisms underlying this species' extreme longevity and low reproductive output may offer insights into the evolution of life-history strategies in marine vertebrates facing rapidly changing oceanographic conditions.
